gancho: O francês que levou à indústria a conserva em vidro fervido recebeu 12 mil francos do governo para revelar o método, meio século antes de Pasteur explicar por que funcionava. Morreu pobre, em cova de indigente.
explicacao: No fim do século XVIII, os exércitos grandes dependiam de comida que aguentasse a marcha, e a falta dela limitava as campanhas ao verão e ao outono. Por isso o governo francês ofereceu um prêmio de 12 mil francos a quem achasse um jeito barato de conservar alimentos para a Grande Armée. Nicolas Appert, confeiteiro e cervejeiro, punha a comida em garrafas de vidro, fechava com rolha e cera e fervia tudo em água. Donas de casa talvez já fizessem algo parecido, mas ele foi o primeiro a fazer isso em escala industrial. Em 1804, sua casa em Massy, perto de Paris, virou a primeira fábrica de alimentos engarrafados do mundo. Em 1810, o Ministério do Interior lhe pagou os 12 mil francos com a condição de que publicasse o processo, e ele lançou um livro com 6 mil exemplares. Appert nunca entendeu de fato por que o método dava certo: a bacteriologia ainda não existia, e só cerca de 50 anos depois Pasteur mostraria o papel dos micróbios na deterioração. A fama não virou dinheiro. Mau negociante, ele faliu em 1806, teve a fábrica destruída por tropas prussianas e austríacas em 1814 e morreu na pobreza em 1841, enterrado em cova de indigente.

fontes.trecho: He placed the food in glass jars, sealed them with cork and sealing wax and placed them in boiling water [...] In 1804, La Maison Appert (English: The House of Appert), in the town of Massy, near Paris, became the first food bottling factory in the world, years before Louis Pasteur proved that heat killed bacteria. [...] he was not a very good businessman. He declared bankruptcy in 1806, but was able to continue his business. In 1795, the French army had offered a prize of 12,000 francs for a new method to preserve food. [...] In 1810 the Bureau of Arts and Manufactures of the Ministry of the Interior gave Appert an ex gratia payment of 12,000 francs on condition that he make his process public. Appert accepted and published a book describing his process that year. [...] 6,000 copies of which were printed in 1810. [...] Appert never truly understood why his method worked, as the science of bacteriology had not yet been developed [...] exacerbated by the destruction of his factory at Massy by Prussian and Austrian forces at the end of the War of the Sixth Coalition in 1814. [...] he died in poverty in 1841 and was buried in a pauper's grave. [...] It is believed that this technique was already being used by homemakers, but Appert was the first to do this on an industrial scale.

the French government offered a hefty cash award of 12,000 francs to any inventor who could devise a cheap and effective method of preserving large amounts of food to create well-preserved military rations for the Grande Armée. The larger armies of the period required increased and regular supplies of quality food. Limited food availability was among the factors limiting military campaigns to the summer and autumn months. In 1809, Nicolas Appert, a French confectioner and brewer [...] The reason for lack of spoilage was unknown at the time, since it would be another 50 years before Louis Pasteur demonstrated the role of microbes in food spoilage

gancho: A lata de conserva foi patenteada em 1810, mas o primeiro abridor só surgiu em 1855. As primeiras latas traziam a instrução de abrir a tampa com martelo e talhadeira.
explicacao: A conserva em lata é até mais antiga que a patente: a Marinha holandesa já usava comida enlatada desde pelo menos 1772. Em 1810, o inglês Peter Durand patenteou o método, e em 1813 Bryan Donkin abriu em Londres a primeira fábrica de enlatados do mundo. As primeiras latas eram de ferro estanhado, tão robustas que pesavam mais que a comida dentro delas, e abri-las exigia criatividade. Os rótulos mandavam cortar em volta da tampa, rente à borda, com talhadeira e martelo. Só em 1855 o cuteleiro inglês Robert Yeates criou um abridor em forma de garra, que ia rasgando o metal; em 1858 veio, nos EUA, o de Ezra Warner, uma lâmina curva serrada em volta da borda. O abridor com roda cortante giratória apareceu em 1870, mas era difícil de usar, e o modelo fácil, com uma segunda roda dentada para prender a borda, só chegou em 1925. Uma explicação para a demora de décadas é que as ferramentas que já existiam davam conta do recado, e criar uma nova custava caro. As latas foram ficando mais finas com o tempo, mas nem assim surgiu logo um abridor de uso geral.

fontes.trecho: Food preserved in tin cans was in use by the Dutch Navy from at least 1772. [...] Preservation of food in tin cans was patented by Peter Durand in 1810. That patent was acquired in 1812 by Bryan Donkin, who soon set up the world's first canning factory in London in 1813. [...] The first cans were robust containers, which weighed more than the food they contained and required ingenuity to open, using whatever tools available. The instruction on those cans read "Cut round the top near the outer edge with a chisel and hammer." The gap of decades between the invention of the can and can opener may be attributed to the functionality of existing tools versus the cost and effort of developing a new tool. [...] Can walls became thinner, but there still was no general-purpose can opener. [...] In 1855, Robert Yeates, a cutlery and surgical instrument maker [...] devised the first claw-ended can opener with a hand-operated tool that haggled its way around the top of metal cans. In 1858, another lever-type opener of a more complex shape was patented in the United States by Ezra Warner of Waterbury, Connecticut, US. It consisted of a sharp sickle, which was pushed into the can and sawed around its edge. [...] A can opener using the now familiar rotating cutting wheel that runs round the can's rim to cut open the lid was invented in 1870, but the first such design was considered very difficult to operate for the ordinary consumer. A more successful design came out in 1925 when a second, opposing wheel was added, with a serrated surface to grip the rim of the can
Bryan Donkin developed the process of packaging food in sealed airtight cans, made of tinned wrought iron.

gancho: A expedição Franklin sumiu no Ártico a partir de 1845, e ninguém voltou. Ossos com muito chumbo puseram a culpa nas latas mal soldadas, mas estudos de 2013 e 2016 contestam: talvez faltasse zinco.
explicacao: Os dois navios de John Franklin partiram em busca da Passagem do Noroeste com comida para três anos, incluindo sopas e legumes em lata, carne salgada e pemmican. As 8 mil latas vieram de um fornecedor contratado só sete semanas antes da partida, e a pressa cobrou seu preço: a solda de chumbo de algumas era grossa e malfeita, escorrida pelo lado de dentro. Frio, fome e doenças mataram todos. Nos anos 1980, o antropólogo Owen Beattie achou em ossos de um tripulante 226 partes por milhão de chumbo, dez vezes mais que em esqueletos de inuítes da mesma região, e a ideia de que as latas envenenaram a tripulação ganhou o mundo. Depois vieram as críticas: a Marinha britânica usava latas havia anos sem surto de saturnismo, e outra suspeita era o sistema de dessalinização dos navios. Em 2013, um estudo viu que o chumbo nos ossos tinha sido constante ao longo da vida dos marinheiros, sem o pico esperado nos últimos meses. Em 2016, a análise de uma unha de John Hartnell mostrou chumbo normal até as últimas semanas e zinco muito baixo, sinal de desnutrição. A doença teria liberado no sangue o chumbo guardado no corpo. O peso de cada causa segue em debate.

fontes.trecho: Hypothermia, starvation, lead poisoning or zinc deficiency and diseases including scurvy, along with general exposure to a hostile environment while lacking adequate clothing and nutrition, killed everyone on the expedition in the years after it was last sighted by a whaling ship in July 1845. [...] three years' supply of food, which included tinned soup and vegetables, salt-cured meat, pemmican, and several live cattle. The tinned food was supplied from a provisioner, Stephen Goldner, who was awarded the contract on 1 April 1845, a mere seven weeks before Franklin set sail. Goldner worked frantically on the large order of 8,000 tins. The haste required affected quality control of some of the tins, which were later found to have lead soldering that was "thick and sloppily done, and dripped like melted candle wax down the inside surface". [...] The analysis would find an unexpected level of 226 parts per million (ppm) of lead in the crewman's bones, which was ten times higher than the control samples, taken from Inuit skeletons from the same geographic area, of 26–36 ppm. [...] After returning to Edmonton in 1982 and learning of the lead level findings from the 1981 expedition, Beattie struggled to find a cause. [...] Subsequent research has suggested that another potential source for the lead may have been the ships' distilled water systems rather than the tinned food. [...] In addition, tinned food was in widespread use within the Royal Navy at that time and its use did not lead to any significant increase in lead poisoning elsewhere. [...] A 2013 study determined that the levels of lead present in the crew members' bones had been consistent during their lives [...] both the concentration of lead and its isotopic composition would have been expected to have "spiked" during their last few months. This interpretation was supported by a 2016 study that suggested the crew's ill health may in fact have been due to malnutrition, and specifically zinc deficiency, probably due to a lack of meat in their diet. This study used micro-X-ray fluorescence to map the levels of lead, copper and zinc in Hartnell's thumbnail over the final months of his life, and found that apart from during his last few weeks lead concentrations within Hartnell's body were within healthy limits. In contrast, levels of zinc were far lower than normal [...] his illness would have caused his body to start breaking down bone, fat and muscle tissues, releasing lead previously stored there into his bloodstream

Studies in the 1980s attributed the lead from the cans as a factor in the disastrous outcome of the 1845 Franklin expedition to chart and navigate the Northwest Passage. However, studies in 2013 and 2016 suggested that lead poisoning was likely not a factor

gancho: O pemmican, carne seca socada e misturada com gordura, criado por indígenas da América do Norte, era tão vital no comércio de peles que proibir sua exportação de uma colônia, em 1814, desencadeou a "Guerra do Pemmican".
explicacao: O nome vem da palavra cree pimîhkân, derivada de pimî, "gordura". A carne de bisão, cervo ou alce era cortada fina e seca no fogo baixo ou ao sol até ficar quebradiça; cerca de 5 libras de carne fresca davam 1 libra de carne seca. Moída quase até virar pó, era misturada com gordura derretida, mais ou menos meio a meio, às vezes com frutinhas, e guardada em sacos de couro cru. O resultado, denso em calorias, alimentava os remadores do comércio de peles, que não tinham tempo de caçar no curto verão sem gelo. Os métis, de origem mista, caçavam bisões nas pradarias, faziam pemmican e o vendiam aos postos da Companhia do Noroeste. Em 1814, com falta de comida na Colônia do Rio Vermelho, ligada à rival Companhia da Baía de Hudson, o governador Miles Macdonell proibiu a saída de pemmican da região. Métis e a Companhia do Noroeste reagiram, e o conflito entre as duas empresas só acabou em 1821, quando uma absorveu a outra. Num dos choques, a Batalha de Seven Oaks, que durou 25 minutos, morreram 21 colonos e empregados da Baía de Hudson. Mais tarde, o pemmican foi comida de exploradores polares como Amundsen, Scott e Shackleton.

fontes.trecho: The name comes from the Cree word ᐱᒦᐦᑳᓐ (pimîhkân), which is derived from the word ᐱᒥᕀ (pimî), 'fat, grease'. [...] It was invented by the Indigenous peoples of North America. Pemmican was widely adopted as a concentrated high-calorie food by Europeans involved in the fur trade and later by Arctic and Antarctic explorers, such as Captain Robert Bartlett, Ernest Shackleton, Richard E. Byrd, Fridtjof Nansen, Robert Falcon Scott, George W. DeLong, Robert Peary, Matthew Henson, and Roald Amundsen. [...] large game meat such as bison, deer, elk, or moose [...] Traditionally, the meat was cut in thin slices and dried, either over a slow fire or in the hot sun, until it was hard and brittle. Approximately 5 pounds of fresh meat make 1 pound of dried meat suitable for pemmican. [...] beaten with flails or ground between two large stones until it turned into very small pieces, almost powder-like in its consistency. The pounded meat was then mixed with melted fat in an approximate 1:1 ratio by weight. [...] The resulting mixture was then packed into rawhide bags for storage [...] The voyageurs of the North American fur trade had no time to live off the land during the short season when the lakes and rivers were free of ice. [...] Trading people of mixed ancestry who would become known as the Métis people would go southwest onto the prairie in Red River carts, slaughter bison, convert it into pemmican, and carry it north to trade from settlements they would make adjacent to North West Company posts. [...] So important was pemmican that, in 1814, governor Miles Macdonell started the Pemmican War with the Métis when he passed the short-lived Pemmican Proclamation, which forbade the export of pemmican from the Red River Colony.

The Pemmican War  was a series of interactions through violent confrontations between the Hudson's Bay Company (HBC) and the North West Company (NWC) in the Canadas from 1812 to 1821. It started after the establishment of the Red River Colony by Thomas Douglas, 5th Earl of Selkirk in 1812, and ended in 1821 when the NWC was merged into the HBC. [...] This was fiercely opposed by the Métis, who were mostly affiliated with the NWC [...] Provisions were scarce in the colony at the beginning of 1814. [...] The battle lasted only 25 minutes. In the end, 21 Red River settlers and Hudson's Bay Company employees were killed, including Governor Semple [...] This event would come to be known as the Battle of Seven Oaks

gancho: O "sorvete de astronauta" das lojas de museu talvez nunca tenha ido ao espaço. Só aparece num cardápio da Apollo 7, de 1968, e o tripulante que falou do assunto não se lembrava dele. Sorvete comum, sim, já voou.
explicacao: O sorvete liofilizado foi desenvolvido pela Whirlpool sob contrato da NASA, na época do programa Apollo. Na liofilização, o sorvete é congelado numa câmara, a pressão cai abaixo do ponto triplo da água e um pouco de calor faz o gelo passar direto a vapor, sem derreter. Sobra um bloco seco e quebradiço que não derrete à temperatura ambiente. A NASA usava alimentos liofilizados desde as bebidas em pó do programa Mercury, e na era Apollo os astronautas tinham mais de 60 itens assim. Mas o sorvete não pegou. A única evidência de que tenha voado é o kit de imprensa da Apollo 7, que lista "sorvete de baunilha" num dos cardápios. Em 2019, Walt Cunningham, então o último tripulante vivo dessa missão, disse não se lembrar dele a bordo; os outros dois morreram sem comentar. Já um artigo do Museu Nacional do Ar e do Espaço, do Smithsonian, afirma que ele foi servido na Apollo 7. O produto vendido hoje surgiu em 1974, quando uma empresa de comida de acampamento foi procurada para fazer algo que um museu pudesse vender como lembrança. Enquanto isso, astronautas comeram sorvete congelado de verdade nos anos 1970, no Skylab, que tinha freezer, e também na Estação Espacial Internacional.

fontes.trecho: Compared to regular ice cream, it can be kept at room temperature without melting, is dry and more brittle and rigid [...] It was developed by Whirlpool Corporation under contract to NASA for the Apollo missions. [...] The ice cream is first placed in a vacuum chamber and frozen until any remaining water crystallizes. The air pressure is then lowered below water's triple point [...] next, heat is applied, sublimating the ice [...] During the 1970s, astronauts ate regular ice cream on the Skylab space station; it has also been eaten on the International Space Station. Skylab had a freezer that was used for regular ice cream [...] The only evidence for freeze-dried ice cream ever having flown in space is the menu for the Apollo 7 mission, on which it is listed for one of the meals. [...] According to one NASA food scientist, although freeze-dried ice cream was developed on request, "it wasn't that popular."

fontes.titulo: Astronaut ice cream turns 50: freeze-dried treat still popular (even if it never flew)
fontes.trecho: was first introduced in 1974 by American Outdoor Products. [...] They wanted to know if we could make it so they could sell it in their gift shop. [...] NASA first turned to the freeze-drying process for the powdered drinks flown on the Mercury orbital missions in the early 1960s. [...] By the time the Apollo moon program began, the astronauts could choose from more than 60 different freeze-dried, bite-size items. [...] In NASA's 1968 press kit for its first three-man launch, NASA listed "vanilla ice cream" on one of the three menus for the Apollo 7 astronauts. It is the only known instance that freeze-dried ice cream has appeared on a NASA-prepared menu. [...] In 2019, the then-last surviving member of the Apollo 7 crew was asked about the ice cream. Walt Cunningham said he did not remember having it on the mission. [...] Wally Schirra, commander of Apollo 7, died in 2007, and command module pilot Donn Eisele died in 1987, each without ever commenting publicly on the topic.

fontes.titulo: We All Scream - Even in Space - for Ice Cream (National Air and Space Museum)
fontes.trecho: The gift-shop staple, “Astronaut Ice Cream,” was the first type of ice cream to make it into space during the Apollo 7 mission in 1968, and it was the only time it was “served” in space.

gancho: A história do mel de milênios achado comestível em tumbas do Egito não se sustenta. Um pote de "mel ainda líquido" que espantou um egiptólogo era, pela análise química, óleo de rícino que tinha azedado.
explicacao: O mel resiste mesmo ao tempo: as abelhas o deixam com só 15,5% a 18% de água, e tanto açúcar dissolvido em tão pouca água impede que micróbios se multipliquem. Elas ainda misturam ao néctar uma enzima, a glicose oxidase, que gera ácido glucônico e peróxido de hidrogênio. Daí nasceu a história de potes de mel achados em tumbas egípcias e ainda bons para comer. Num artigo científico, o egiptólogo F. Filce Leek reexaminou os casos. O inspetor de antiguidades Arthur Weigall descreveu, em carta à família, quase ter desmaiado ao ver na tumba de Yuya e Tuya um jarro de alabastro com mel ainda líquido, com "três mil e quinhentos anos". O químico Alfred Lucas fez mais de doze testes no conteúdo do vaso e concluiu que era óleo de rícino muito ácido. Na tumba de Tutancâmon, dois jarros com a inscrição "mel de boa qualidade" estavam quase vazios, e o resto seco só lembrou caramelo. Leek ainda pediu amostras a museus: uma era cera, outra, um líquido preto sem nenhum grão de pólen, ou seja, não era mel. Ele concluiu que, tirando um favo, faltava confirmação por pólen para o mel dado como achado nas tumbas.

fontes.titulo: Some evidence of bees and honey in ancient Egypt (F. Filce Leek, Bee World, 1975)
fontes.trecho: The author of this article is an Egyptologist [...] two pottery jars bearing the hieratic inscription "honey of good quality" that were found by Howard Carter [...] they were practically empty, except for a trace of dried material adhering to the inside. [...] the only indication of sugar being a slight smell suggestive of caramel (burnt sugar) [...] a letter written by the late Arthur E. Weigall, one-time Inspector-General of Antiquities to the Egyptian Government, to members of his family in England, describing his impressions during the opening of the tomb of Yusa and Thuiu [...] among them was an alabaster jug full of honey still liquid. When I saw this I nearly fainted [...] yet three thousand five hundred years old [...] Lucas [...] gives particulars of more than twelve chemical and analytical tests he applied to the sample. In his conclusion, he states: "From the results obtained there can be little doubt that the sample is Castor Oil that has become very acid [...] It seems to be accepted as a fact that many samples of honey have been recovered from ancient Egyptian tombs ever since the pyramid age, but apart from one sample of honeycomb examined by Zander [...] authentication by pollen analysis is lacking. [...] Dissolved in ether, therefore a wax [...] A black sticky liquid taken from an Eighteenth Dynasty vase, no pollen grains whatsoever, consequently not honey.

final water content of between 15.5% and 18%. [...] For osmotic reasons such high concentrations of sugar are extremely unfavorable to microbiological reproduction and all fermentation is consequently halted. [...] (However, no edible honey has been found in Egyptian tombs; all such cases have been proven to be other substances or only chemical traces.) [...] The bees mix glucose oxidase with expelled nectar they previously consumed, creating two byproducts – gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide, which are partially responsible for honey acidity and suppression of bacterial growth.

gancho: Já em 1906, uma patente britânica propunha conservar comida com radiação, dez anos após a descoberta da radioatividade. Hoje mais de 60 países permitem a técnica, e no Brasil qualquer alimento pode ser irradiado.
explicacao: A radioatividade natural foi descoberta por Becquerel em 1896, e em 1906 os britânicos Appleby e Banks já patenteavam o uso de isótopos radioativos para irradiar alimentos. A ideia é expor a comida, muitas vezes já embalada, a raios gama de cobalto-60, a feixes de elétrons ou a raios X. Isso reduz os organismos que estragam a comida, atrasa o amadurecimento e impede que batata, cebola e alho brotem. Mesmo assim, a comida não fica radioativa: a energia das fontes usadas é limitada por lei, baixa demais para alterar o núcleo dos átomos do alimento, por mais partículas que o atinjam. A NASA irradia itens da comida dos astronautas desde 1963, e a carne congelada deles recebe doses bem acima das permitidas no comércio. A prática é liberada em mais de 60 países, que tratam cerca de 500 mil toneladas por ano, mas as regras variam muito. Na Alemanha, na Áustria e em vários países da União Europeia, só ervas secas, especiarias e temperos podem ser irradiados; no Brasil, qualquer alimento pode ser tratado. Na União Europeia, em 2021, os itens mais irradiados foram coxas de rã, seguidas de aves.

fontes.trecho: Food irradiation is permitted in over 60 countries, and about 500,000 metric tons of such food are  processed annually worldwide. The regulations for how food is to be irradiated, as well as the foods allowed to be irradiated, vary greatly from country to country. In Austria, Germany, and many other countries of the European Union only dried herbs, spices, and seasonings can be processed with irradiation and only at a specific dose, while in Brazil all foods are allowed at any dose. [...] Irradiation slows the speed at which enzymes change the food. By reducing or removing spoilage organisms and slowing ripening and sprouting (e.g. potato, onion, and garlic) irradiation is used to reduce the amount of food that goes bad between harvest and final use. Shelf-stable products are created by irradiating foods in sealed packages [...] Irradiated food does not become radioactive; only particle energies that are incapable of causing significant induced radioactivity are used for food irradiation. In the United States this limit is 4 mega electron volts (MEV) for electron beams and x-ray sources—cobalt-60 or caesium-137 sources are never energetic enough to induce radioactivity. Particles below this energy can never be energetic enough to modify the nucleus of the targeted atom in the food, regardless of how many particles hit the target material [...] High-dose applications are above those currently permitted in the US for commercial food items by the FDA and other regulators around the world, though these doses are approved for non commercial applications, such as sterilizing frozen meat for NASA astronauts (doses of 44 kGy) [...] Radiation may be emitted by a radioactive substance, or by X-ray and electron beam accelerators. [...] Gamma irradiation is produced from the radioisotopes cobalt-60 and caesium-137 [...] Cobalt-60 is the most common source of gamma rays for food irradiation in commercial scale facilities [...] In 2021 the most common food items irradiated were frog legs at 65.1%, poultry 20.6% and dried aromatic herbs, spices and vegetables seasoning. [...] 1896 Antoine Henri Becquerel discovers natural radioactivity [...] 1906 Appleby & Banks: UK patent to use radioactive isotopes to irradiate particulate food in a flowing bed [...] 1963 FDA approves food irradiation. NASA begins irradiating astronaut food items to prevent food borne illness during space missions.

gancho: A pasteurização foi criada para o vinho, não para o leite. Em 1864, Pasteur viu que aquecer vinho novo a uns 50–60 °C impedia que azedasse. E na China já se aquecia vinho para conservá-lo desde o ano 1117.
explicacao: Louis Pasteur passava as férias de verão de 1864 em Arbois, terra de vinhos que muitas vezes azedavam ao envelhecer. Em experimentos, viu que bastava aquecer o vinho jovem a cerca de 50 a 60 °C por pouco tempo para matar os micróbios responsáveis, e que depois a bebida envelhecia sem perder qualidade. Era um método mais suave que o de Nicolas Appert, que fervia a comida em potes fechados. Durante anos, a pasteurização serviu para evitar que vinho e cerveja azedassem, e muito tempo se passaria até que o leite fosse pasteurizado: a ideia foi sugerida pelo químico Franz von Soxhlet só em 1886. Em 1910, Nova York tornou obrigatória a pasteurização do leite. Pasteur também não foi o primeiro a usar calor no vinho. Na China, aquecer vinho para conservá-lo era conhecido desde o ano 1117, e no Japão a prática foi registrada num diário mantido por monges entre 1478 e 1618. O que Pasteur trouxe foi a explicação: os culpados eram micro-organismos, e para eliminá-los não era preciso ferver o vinho; um aquecimento curto e moderado bastava.

fontes.trecho: Heating wine for preservation has been known in China since AD 1117 and was documented in Japan in the diary Tamonin-nikki written by a series of monks between 1478 and 1618. [...] A less aggressive method was developed by French chemist Louis Pasteur during an 1864 summer holiday in Arbois. To remedy the frequent acidity of the local aged wines, he found out experimentally that it is sufficient to heat a young wine to only about 50–60 °C (122–140 °F) for a short time to kill the microbes, and that the wine could subsequently be aged without sacrificing the final quality. [...] Pasteurization was originally used as a way of preventing wine and beer from souring, and it would be many years before milk was pasteurized. [...] In 1910, Lederle, then in the role of Commissioner of Health, introduced mandatory pasteurization of milk in New York City. [...] Pasteurization of milk was suggested by Franz von Soxhlet in 1886.

gancho: O congelado de supermercado nasceu de uma lição dos inuítes. No Labrador, a −40 °C, Clarence Birdseye viu peixe recém-pescado congelar quase na hora e, descongelado, ainda parecer fresco. O segredo era a pressa.
explicacao: Birdseye era naturalista do Departamento de Agricultura dos EUA e passou temporadas no Labrador, entre 1912 e 1915. Ali, os inuítes lhe ensinaram a pescar sob gelo muito grosso e mostraram que, no frio de −40 °C, o peixe exposto ao ar congelava instantaneamente e, ao descongelar, mantinha o gosto de fresco. O peixe congelado vendido em Nova York era bem pior. A explicação física está nos cristais de gelo. Congelar devagar dá tempo para a água formar cristais de gelo grandes, que rasgam os tecidos; no degelo, o suco das células escorre e a comida fica mole ou ressecada. Num frio intenso, o congelamento é tão rápido que só se formam cristais pequenos, e o estrago é bem menor. A primeira empresa de Birdseye faliu em 1924 por falta de interesse do público. Ele insistiu: criou máquinas que congelavam o peixe já embalado, prensado entre superfícies geladas. Em 1929, vendeu a empresa e as patentes por 22 milhões de dólares ao grupo que viraria a General Foods, e em 1930 os congelados foram testados em 18 lojas de Springfield, em Massachusetts. Esse teste é considerado o nascimento do congelado no varejo.

fontes.trecho: he worked for the United States Department of Agriculture as a field naturalist and conducted wildlife surveys in the American West and Labrador. [...] Birdseye's next field assignment, intermittently from 1912 to 1915, was in Labrador [...] He was taught by the Inuit how to ice fish under very thick ice. In −40 °C (−40 °F) weather, the Inuit also demonstrated that freshly caught fish could be then instantly flash frozen when exposed to air, and when thawed, still tasted fresh. He recognized the potential that this traditional knowledge held if it were to be employed in production since the frozen seafood sold in New York was of lower quality than the frozen fish of Labrador. [...] When food is frozen slowly, at temperatures near the freezing point, ice crystals form within the animal or vegetable cells; when the food thaws, cellular fluid leaks from the damaged tissue, giving the food a mushy or dry consistency. Rapid freezing, at lower temperatures, gives crystals less time to form and thus does less damage. [...] In 1924, his company went bankrupt for lack of consumer interest in the product. That same year, he developed an entirely new process for commercially viable quick-freezing: packing fish in cartons, then freezing the contents between two refrigerated surfaces under pressure. [...] In 1929, Birdseye sold his company and patents to Goldman Sachs and the Postum Company which eventually became General Foods Corporation [...] offered him $22 million [...] In 1930, the company began sales experiments in 18 retail stores around Springfield, Massachusetts, to test consumer acceptance of quick-frozen foods. [...] today this is considered the birth of retail frozen foods.

gancho: No arenque fermentado sueco, o surströmming, a lata estufada é normal: bactérias seguem trabalhando lá dentro e soltam gás. Num incêndio num depósito em 2014, mil latas explodiram em seis horas.
explicacao: O surströmming, "arenque azedo", é feito no norte da Suécia desde pelo menos o século XVI com arenque do Báltico. O truque é usar só o sal necessário para o peixe não apodrecer, mas deixá-lo fermentar. A salmoura cria uma pressão osmótica alta demais para as bactérias da putrefação, mas boa para bactérias do gênero Halanaerobium, que transformam o glicogênio do peixe em ácidos. A fermentação dura ao menos seis meses e continua depois de enlatada. Na lata, essas bactérias soltam gás carbônico e os compostos do cheiro famoso: ácido propiônico, gás sulfídrico (de ovo podre), ácido butírico (de manteiga rançosa) e ácido acético (de vinagre). Por isso a lata incha bastante, algo que numa conserva comum seria sinal de alerta para contaminação. Em 2006, várias companhias aéreas, como Air France e British Airways, proibiram o peixe a bordo por medo de explosões; os produtores chamaram a decisão de "culturalmente analfabeta" e o risco de mito. Num incêndio num depósito sueco em 2014, porém, mil latas estouraram em seis horas. Até hoje, as lojas respeitam a "estreia" da safra na terceira quinta-feira de agosto, herança de uma norma dos anos 1940.

fontes.trecho: Swedish for 'sour herring') is a lightly salted, fermented Baltic Sea herring traditional to Swedish cuisine since at least the 16th century. [...] During the production of surströmming, just enough salt is used to prevent the raw herring from rotting while allowing it to ferment. A fermentation process of at least six months gives the fish its characteristic strong smell and somewhat acidic taste. [...] At the end of the 1940s, surströmming producers in Sweden lobbied for a royal ordinance [...] forbade sales of the current year's production in Sweden prior to the third Thursday in August. While the ordinance is no longer in force, retailers still maintain the date for the "premiere" of that year's catch. [...] Surströmming has been part of northern Swedish cuisine since at least the 16th century. [...] The salt raises the osmotic pressure of the brine above the zone where bacteria responsible for rotting can thrive [...] the osmotic conditions enable Halanaerobium bacteria such as H. praevalens to thrive and decompose the fish glycogen into organic acids, making it sour (acidic). [...] Fermentation continues in the can, causing it to bulge noticeably, which would usually be a sign of botulism or other food poisoning concern in non-fermented canned foods. Species of Halanaerobium bacteria are responsible for the in-can ripening. These bacteria produce carbon dioxide and a number of compounds that account for the unique odor: pungent (propionic acid), rotten-egg (hydrogen sulfide), rancid-butter (butyric acid), and vinegary (acetic acid). Due to these gases, a thousand cans of surströmming exploded over a period of six hours during a fire at a Swedish warehouse in 2014. [...] In April 2006, several major airlines (such as Air France, British Airways, Finnair and KLM) banned the fish, claiming that the pressurised cans of fish are potentially explosive. [...] Those who produce the fish have called the airlines' decision "culturally illiterate", claiming that it is a "myth that the tinned fish can explode".

gancho: O ovo centenário chinês não leva cem anos nem é curtido em urina de cavalo, como diz um mito. Semanas ou meses numa pasta alcalina elevam seu pH a 9–12, e a clara vira um gel marrom e translúcido.
explicacao: O pídàn, feito com ovos de pata, galinha ou codorna, é envolto numa mistura de argila, cinzas, sal, cal virgem e casca de arroz. O que transforma o ovo é um sal alcalino, que vai subindo o pH até a faixa de 9 a 12 durante a cura, de semanas a meses. Esse ambiente quebra parte das proteínas e gorduras em compostos menores e saborosos. A clara fica marrom-escura, gelatinosa e translúcida, com gosto salgado e umami; a gema, cinza-esverdeada, cremosa e de sabor forte, por causa do gás sulfídrico e da amônia. O cheiro de amônia talvez explique o mito da urina: em tailandês e em laosiano, o nome comum do ovo se traduz como "ovo de urina de cavalo". O método provavelmente surgiu para guardar ovos em época de fartura, e existe na culinária chinesa pelo menos desde o século XVII. Lendas contam que ovos esquecidos em cal de construção ou num buraco de cinzas foram achados transformados. A fabricação industrial já teve escândalos: em 2013, fábricas da província de Jiangxi usavam sulfato de cobre industrial contaminado para acelerar o processo, e 30 fábricas foram fechadas para inspeção.

fontes.trecho: is a Chinese dish made by preserving duck, chicken, or quail eggs in a mixture of clay, ash, salt, quicklime, and rice hulls for several weeks to several months, depending on the processing method. Through the process, the yolk becomes dark greenish-grey in color, with a smooth consistency and strong flavor due to the hydrogen sulfide and ammonia present, while the white becomes dark brown in color, with a translucent jelly-like appearance, a gelatinous texture, and a salty and umami flavor. The transforming agent in the century egg is an alkaline salt, which gradually raises the pH of the egg to around 9–12 during the curing process. This chemical process breaks down some of the complex, flavorless proteins and fats, producing a variety of smaller flavorful compounds. [...] The method for creating century eggs likely came about through the need to preserve eggs in times of plenty [...] The century egg is known to have been present in Chinese cuisine since at least the 17th century CE and its purported origins are the subject of several folk tales. In one such tale, a homeowner living in Hunan during the Ming Dynasty discovered duck eggs in a shallow pool of slaked lime that was used for mortar [...] The eggs were not discovered until the woman cleaned out the ash pit half a month later [...] There is a misconception that century eggs are prepared by soaking eggs in horse urine, but this is not true. In Thai and Lao, the common word for century egg translates to "horse urine egg", due to this misconception or due to the eggs' ammonia odor [...] In 2013, three factories in Jiangxi province were found to be using industrial copper sulphate in century egg production to shorten the production time. The industrial copper sulphate was contaminated with heavy metals and toxic chemicals. The incident was exposed on China's national broadcaster CCTV, causing local officials to shut down 30 factories for inspection.

gancho: Einstein patenteou uma geladeira. Com o ex-aluno Leó Szilárd, criou um modelo sem peças móveis depois de ler que uma família de Berlim morrera com o gás tóxico que vazou da vedação da geladeira de casa.
explicacao: Entre 1926 e 1934, Einstein e Szilárd trabalharam para melhorar a refrigeração doméstica. As geladeiras da época usavam gases tóxicos, e a notícia da família morta em Berlim os convenceu de que um aparelho sem partes móveis eliminaria o risco de a vedação falhar. O modelo mais conhecido é de absorção: funciona com pressão constante, só precisa de uma fonte de calor e usa água, amônia e butano, a partir de um projeto anterior de engenheiros suecos. Einstein, que tinha trabalhado no escritório de patentes da Suíça, cuidou dos pedidos, e a dupla obteve 45 patentes em seis países, para três modelos. Há quem diga que Szilárd inventou quase tudo e Einstein foi consultor; outros afirmam que ele também projetou. A geladeira nunca fez sucesso: era menos eficiente que as rivais, a chegada do Freon, que substituiu os gases tóxicos, tirou seu atrativo, e a Grande Depressão e a perseguição nazista aos dois, que eram judeus, fizeram o resto. A Electrolux comprou as patentes mais promissoras, e a dupla ganhou 750 dólares. Uma bomba eletromagnética criada no projeto foi usada depois para resfriar reatores nucleares.

fontes.trecho: is an absorption refrigerator which has no moving parts, operates at constant pressure, and requires only a heat source to operate. It was jointly invented in 1926 by Albert Einstein and his former student Leó Szilárd [...] The three working fluids in this design are water, ammonia, and butane. The Einstein–Szilárd refrigerator was actually a modification of an earlier three-fluid absorption design created by Swedish engineers Baltzar von Platen and Carl Munters [...] From 1926 until 1934 Einstein and Szilárd collaborated on ways to improve home refrigeration technology. The two were motivated by contemporary newspaper reports of a Berlin family who had been killed when a seal in their refrigerator failed and leaked toxic fumes into their home. Einstein and Szilárd proposed that a device without moving parts would eliminate the potential for seal failure [...] Einstein had worked in the Swiss Patent Office, and used his experience to apply for valid patents for their inventions in several countries. The two were eventually granted 45 patents in six countries for three different models. It has been suggested that most of the actual inventing was done by Szilárd, with Einstein merely acting as a consultant and helping with the patent-related paperwork, but others assert that Einstein contributed design work to the project. The refrigerator was less efficient than existing appliances [...] the introduction of Freon to replace refrigerant gases toxic to humans made it even less attractive commercially. The Great Depression of 1929 dried up funding for development, and the widespread political violence in Nazi Germany, where the inventors lived, particularly towards Jews such as Einstein and Szilard, contributed to the device's lack of commercial success. [...] the most promising of the patents were quickly bought up by the Swedish company Electrolux. Einstein and Szilárd earned $750 [...] the Einstein–Szilard pump was later used for cooling breeder reactors

gancho: Um professor nigeriano pôs um pote de barro dentro de outro, com areia molhada no meio: a água que evapora leva o calor embora. Sem eletricidade, berinjelas duravam 27 dias em vez de três, segundo a revista Time.
explicacao: No norte rural da Nigéria, quase ninguém tem geladeira nem eletricidade, e a comida perecível precisava ser consumida logo. Mohammed Bah Abba, professor de uma família de oleiros, criou nos anos 1990 o seu sistema de conservação: um pote de barro pequeno dentro de um maior, o espaço entre eles cheio de areia úmida e um pano molhado por cima. A água da areia atravessa o barro poroso e evapora na superfície externa, e a evaporação tira calor do pote de dentro. Segundo a revista Time, que listou a invenção entre as melhores de 2001, as berinjelas duravam 27 dias em vez de três, e os tomates e pimentões, até três semanas. Abba contratou oleiros desempregados para fazer o primeiro lote de 5 mil pares, que custavam 40 centavos de dólar, e usou os 75 mil dólares do Prêmio Rolex de Empreendedorismo para espalhar a invenção pelo país. O princípio é antigo: afrescos do Egito de cerca de 2500 a.C. mostram escravos abanando jarros de água, talvez para resfriá-los. Mas há limites. Esses resfriadores rendem pouco em clima úmido e funcionam melhor com umidade relativa abaixo de 40% e máximas acima de 25 °C. Também não servem para carne, laticínios e remédios, que exigem menos de 20 °C o tempo todo.

fontes.trecho: It uses a porous outer clay pot (lined with wet sand) containing an inner pot [...] The evaporation of the outer liquid draws heat from the inner pot. [...] There is evidence that evaporative cooling may have been used in North Africa as early as the Old Kingdom of Egypt, circa 2500 BC. Frescoes show slaves fanning water jars, which would increase air flow around porous jars to aid evaporation and cooling the contents. [...] In rural northern Nigeria in the 1990s, Mohamed Bah Abba developed the Pot-in-Pot Preservation Cooling System [...] Abba, who hails from a family of potmakers, tapped into the large unemployed local workforce and hired skilled potmakers to mass-produce the first batch of 5,000 Pot-in-Pots. He received the Rolex Award for Enterprise in 2001 and used his $75,000 award to make the invention available throughout Nigeria. [...] The pots sell at 40 US cents a pair. [...] Evaporative coolers tend to perform poorly or not at all in climates with high ambient humidity [...] they are used in low-humidity climates (less than 40% relative humidity), the temperature is relatively high (maximum daily temperature higher than 25 °C) [...] are not suitable for items that require sustained temperatures below 20 °C (medicine, meat, and dairy products)

fontes.titulo: Food Cooling System - Best Inventions of 2001 (TIME)
fontes.trecho: Best Inventions of 2001 [...] In rural northern Nigeria, there are no refrigerators. Most people don't even have electricity. So perishable food must be eaten immediately, or it will go to waste. Mohammed Bah Abba, a local teacher, has developed an ingenious solution: the Pot-in-Pot Preservation Cooling System. A small earthenware pot is placed inside a larger one, and the space between the two is filled with moist sand. The inner pot is filled with fruit, vegetables or soft drinks; a wet cloth covers the whole thing. As water in the sand evaporates through the surface of the outer pot, it carries heat, drawing it away from the inner core. Eggplants stay fresh for 27 days, instead of the usual three. Tomatoes and peppers last for up to three weeks.

gancho: Há séculos, os persas faziam e guardavam gelo no deserto, sem eletricidade. Tanques rasos, à sombra de muros altos, perdiam calor para o céu seco da noite e congelavam. O gelo durava o verão.
explicacao: O yakhchāl, "poço de gelo" em persa, é uma casa de gelo antiga dos desertos do Irã; muitas, erguidas há séculos, seguem de pé. O sistema tinha três partes. Nos tanques, canais rasos de 40 a 50 cm de profundidade, a água recebia pouco calor: muros de 10 m, às vezes 15 m, no sentido leste-oeste, faziam sombra de dia. À noite, o ar seco quase não devolvia o calor que a água irradiava para cima, que escapava para o espaço, e a evaporação também a esfriava. Assim, as noites frias do deserto bastavam para formar gelo. O gelo ia para a casa de gelo, uma cúpula cônica alta sobre um depósito subterrâneo de até 5.000 m³. O formato cria um efeito chaminé que empurra o ar quente para fora pelo topo. As paredes, de pelo menos dois metros de espessura na base, eram de sarooj, uma argamassa de areia, argila, clara de ovo, cal, pelo de cabra e cinzas. O gelo servia para conservar comida e fazer doces gelados como o faloodeh. No Irã, no Afeganistão e no Tajiquistão, a geladeira elétrica ainda se chama yakhchāl.

fontes.trecho: A yakhchāl (Persian: یخچال, lit. 'Ice pit'; yakh meaning 'ice' and chāl meaning 'pit') is an ancient type of ice house, which produced ice and desserts associated with it, like faloodeh, or sorbets. They are primarily found in the Dasht-e Lut and Dasht-e-Kavir deserts [...] In modern-day Iran, Afghanistan, and Tajikistan the term yakhchāl is also used to refer to modern refrigerators. [...] Records indicate that these structures were built as far back as 400 BCE, and many that were built hundreds of years ago remain standing [...] including preservation of food, to chill treats [...] in some desert climates, like those at high altitudes, temperatures drop below freezing at night. [...] The tall, conical shape of the building is to optimize the solar chimney effect, creating a convection current to guide any remaining heat upward and outside through openings at the very top of the building. [...] large underground spaces up to 5,000 m3 (180,000 cu ft) in volume. The yakhchāl is built of a unique water-resistant mortar called sarooj. This mortar is composed of sand, clay, egg whites, lime, goat hair, and ash in specific proportions [...] The sarooj walls are at least two meters thick at the base. [...] A wall is usually built in an east–west direction near the yakhchāl, often as high as 10 m (33 ft) and sometimes as high as 15 m (49 ft) [...] with a depth of 40 cm (16 in) to 50 cm (20 in), comparable to a reflecting pool. [...] Heat conduction into the pool would be minimal due to the construction of the shade walls throughout the day [...] Evaporation would take heat away from the pools, as with the rest of the yakhchāl. Due to the low moisture content of the air, very little of the heat radiated upwards from the pool would be reflected back to the pool by the air above it, allowing the pool's heat to be largely emitted into space. This meant that ice pools could use the cold of the desert nights and/or radiative cooling to freeze water which would later be transported to storage as ice.

gancho: Em 1974, cientistas abriram latas de comida de um barco a vapor afundado no rio Missouri em 1865. Cor, cheiro e vitaminas tinham piorado, mas não havia sinal de micróbios: a conserva de 109 anos foi julgada segura.
explicacao: O Bertrand subia o rio Missouri levando mercadorias para Virginia City, cidade nascida da corrida do ouro em Montana. Em 1º de abril de 1865, bateu num tronco submerso perto de Omaha e afundou em menos de dez minutos, numa água de 3,7 m. Ninguém morreu, mas quase toda a carga se perdeu. Em 1968, dois caçadores de naufrágios acharam o casco numa reserva federal de vida selvagem e, por lei, entregaram tudo ao governo: mais de 500 mil objetos saíram do porão, hoje expostos num museu da reserva DeSoto, em Iowa. A carga é um retrato da vida em 1865: roupas, ferramentas, uísque, conhaque, remédios e muita comida. Em 1974, a associação americana dos processadores de alimentos testou amostras das latas, com pêssegos em conhaque, ostras, tomates, mel e legumes. Aparência, cheiro e vitaminas tinham se deteriorado, mas não havia nenhum vestígio de crescimento de micróbios, e a comida foi considerada ainda segura para consumo. É o princípio de Appert levado ao extremo: aquecida e bem fechada, a lata não deixa micróbios entrarem.

fontes.trecho: The Bertrand was a steamboat which sank on April 1, 1865, while carrying cargo up the Missouri River to Virginia City, Montana Territory, after hitting a snag in the river north of Omaha, Nebraska. [...] Today, the artifacts are displayed in a museum at the DeSoto National Wildlife Refuge near Missouri Valley, Iowa. [...] When gold was found at the Alder Gulch claim in Montana in 1863 [...] struck a submerged log in the Desoto Bend of the Missouri River, about 25 miles (40 km) upstream of Omaha, Nebraska. In less than ten minutes, it sank in 12 feet (3.7 m) of water. No people died, but almost the entire cargo was lost [...] More than 100 years later, in 1968, private salvagers Sam Corbino and Jesse Pursell discovered the wreck in the DeSoto National Wildlife Refuge [...] Since the boat was found on government property, the men had to comply with the Antiquities Act of 1906, by which they relinquished all of the recovered artifacts to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for permanent preservation. More than 10,000 cubic feet of cargo and over 500,000 artifacts were recovered from the hold during the excavation. The artifacts represent a time capsule of life in 1865 [...] The steamboat was full of clothing, tools, food, and various consumer items on their way upriver. [...] many bottles of whiskey including bourbon; brandy and brandied cherries; and medicine bottles. [...] In 1974, samples of canned food from the wreck, including brandied peaches, oysters, plum tomatoes, honey, and mixed vegetables, were tested by the National Food Processors Association. Although their appearance, smell, and vitamin content had deteriorated, there was no trace of microbial growth and the food was determined to be still safe to eat.

In 1974, samples of canned food from the wreck of the Bertrand, a steamboat that sank in the Missouri River in 1865, were tested by the National Food Processors Association. Although appearance, smell, and vitamin content had deteriorated, there was no trace of microbial growth and the 109-year-old food was determined to be still safe to eat.
